Clustering is unsupervised learning: the algorithm observes data without targets and finds groups of similar items. The result is a finite set of clusters and a rule that assigns new items to one of them, or to several with different weights. In multimedia retrieval, clustering serves four purposes.
reduces a multi-dimensional feature to a small number of discrete values, much like a histogram approximates a distribution.
maps groups of dimensions to a few bits, as product quantization does for vector search.
extracts groups from a collection and infers labels for them.

groups the pixels of an image into regions that belong together: clustering first quantizes the colors, and morphological operators then build coherent regions. This section describes k-means, expectation maximization with Gaussian mixtures, and how to choose the number of clusters.

Compute the new centroids as the means of the items in each cluster.
Repeat steps 2 and 3 until the assignments no longer change.

Neither step can increase the WCSS. Step 2 moves each item to its nearest centroid, and step 3 places each centroid at the point that minimizes the squared distances to its items. The algorithm therefore converges, usually in a few iterations, but the local optimum depends on the initial centroids.

(Arthur and Vassilvitskii 2007) chooses the first centroid at random and each further one among the remaining items with a probability proportional to the squared distance to the nearest centroid chosen so far. Distant items are therefore likely to become centroids. The seeding costs more, but it leads to much smaller final errors and faster convergence, and it is the default in most libraries. Estimating the parameters would be easy if we knew which cluster each item came from: the mean and the variance of each cluster would follow from its items, and the prior from its share of the items. Conversely, if we knew the parameters, Bayes’ rule would give the probability that an item comes from each cluster.

The name comes from the general form of the algorithm. The cluster memberships are
: they are not observed, and the likelihood of the data is a sum over all their possible values, which has no closed-form maximum. EM instead maximizes the
log-likelihood of the data together with the latent variables, where the expectation uses the distribution of the latent variables given the data and the current parameters (the E-step), and the
over the parameters has a closed-form solution (the M-step). Dempster, Laird, and Rubin (1977) showed that this never decreases the likelihood itself.
